#7466. Reddit tests AI-compiled product reviews

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new feature is designed to help users get recommendations and information by converting platform comments into overviews.

Reddit is testing a new Reddit Reviews option, which will help users find relevant product recommendations and info in the app by converting relevant Reddit comments into dedicated overviews.

As shown in these example screens, Reddit Reviews will use artificial intelligence to collate information on products, sourcing relevant references from comments and mentions across the app. The tool will then present comments and upvotes in a centralized review format, which should make it easier for users to gather context about a prospective purchase.

As explained by Reddit: “Lived experience shows up across Reddit communities: in r/skincareaddiction, people share what they’ve tried for dry skin, and in r/espresso, baristas and home brewers compare their setups. These exchanges show how a product can work for different people and what tradeoffs they consider. Reddit Reviews uses AI to both organize these conversations where people describe their product experiences, and to surface the nuance, context, and connection to the original conversation.”

Reddit said these reviews may also include images, prices and purchase links when they’re supplied by brand and retailer catalogs.

“To go deeper, people can browse all comments about a product, using topic filters derived from Reddit conversations to focus on their questions,” Reddit said. “Clicking on a comment lets them read the original discussion, ask a follow-up question, or join the community for more advice. For people considering alternatives, the review also highlights products people commonly compare.”

To find a review, Reddit users can search for a product or category in the app. Products with a review page will be highlighted in the predictive answers to the query.

Reddit said it will initially test the option “with a set of frequently discussed products and categories.”

Reddit added that these reviews will only include information gleaned from organic conversations within Reddit communities, and that these recommendations will not include paid placement of any kind.

Reddit is working to find more ways to get people coming directly to its app for insights because its referral traffic from search engines has been rapidly declining.

Amid rising use of AI chatbots for discovery, Reddit had become a critical source of information due to its user-generated, community-voted listings, which allowed chatbots and search engines to offer direct insights into consumer experiences.

But Google has been putting more emphasis on AI overviews, which provide an AI-generated summary of these notes within search results, while ChatGPT has also reduced its reliance on Reddit data. As a result, Reddit has suffered a big loss in terms of search referrals.

In the company’s Q3 performance update published earlier this month, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said that the company’s search traffic dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week in October.

Given this, Reddit is working to build more valuable tools to drive direct traffic. The company is also experimenting with locking down more of its information, making it only available to logged-in users.

Reddit Reviews is another step in this direction as the platform looks for ways to maintain the value of its app.

#7462. TikTok tests shopping subscriptions

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company invited select users in the U.S. to join its TikTok Shop Plus program, which will cost about $10 a month after a free trial period.

TikTok is trying out another way to get more people shopping in its app with the launch of a new TikTok Shop Plus subscription option that offers discounts and deals for repeat buyers.

As reported by Modern Retail, TikTok began inviting selected U.S. users over the weekend to join its new TikTok Shop Plus program. Additional reporting from GeekSeller suggested that TikTok has been gradually rolling out the option over the last month.

As per Modern Retail: “TikTok Shop Plus costs $9.99 a month after a 30-day free trial, according to TikTok Shop. It includes perks such as expanded free shipping, exclusive discounts, coupon bundles and instant refunds.”

The offering is similar to Amazon Prime and other subscription shopping options, which are designed to increase customer loyalty through add-on benefits.

It’s TikTok’s latest effort to get more people to buy products on the platform as it works to build a bigger revenue stream through in-app shopping.

TikTok owner ByteDance saw significant success with in-stream shopping via Douyin, the version of TikTok available in China. With Douyin, ByteDance was able to successfully transition short-form video engagement into livestream shopping, which has since generated billions of dollars for the company.

According to KrAsia, Douyin generated nearly $500 billion in gross merchandise volume in 2025, with livestream commerce in particular driving a significant portion of that activity.

That’s likely why Douyin has been working to make in-stream shopping a bigger element of the TikTok experience as well. However, TikTok users have so far been less open to shopping in the app.

That may be changing over time, though. According to Marketing Maze, TikTok generated $26.2 billion GMV in the first half of 2025.

That’s still a long way from Douyin’s result, the numbers make it clear why ByteDance is so enamored with the opportunity, and why the company keeps looking for ways to get more people searching for products and making in-stream purchases.

A loyalty program could help on this front by encouraging the most active shoppers to keep buying from TikTok merchants, in the hopes that this will lead to further endorsements and promotions of TikTok’s shopping experience.

Patrick Nommensen, TikTok Shop’s president of strategic initiatives, told Modern Retail that the program is currently being tested “with an expanding group of eligible U.S. users.”

Hands‑on experience building and maintaining highly concurrent, data‑intensive software, with a deep understanding of low‑level network and disk I/O (for example, throughput, latency, backpressure, batching, and failure modes).

#7456. Pepsi’s holiday push includes bigger retail presence, soda for Santa

New ads expand on a “Food Deserves Pepsi” platform that launched in 2024 and positions the soft drink as the ideal pairing with food.

Pepsi is ramping up its marketing activity around the holiday and football seasons, two occasions with a strong connection to food, for efforts that build on a “Food Deserves Pepsi” platform that launched in 2024 and positions the soft drinks as an essential pairing with food. Other moments Pepsi has looked to plug itself into as part of the platform have included soccer viewing parties, barbecues and pizza delivery.

The TV spot will be amplified across a variety of channels and during key moments, including NBC’s holiday tree lighting programming, college football games on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day NBA and NFL games. Additionally, Pepsi expects to have 80% more visibility in retail locations over the year-ago period through holiday packaging, displays, inventory and customer-specific programming throughout the season.

A limited-edition Pepsi Vanilla & Cream Holiday Bundle will be available starting Nov. 19 on Walmart’s website and includes holiday baking items and Pepsi merchandise. Pepsi Vanilla & Cream launched Oct. 18 and has so far received a strong consumer reception, per the brand.

Tapping into football hype, Pepsi launched custom creative featuring Bettis on Nov. 4 across Walmart’s website and social channels. A video, titled “Flag on Flavor,” sees the NFL legend surprising Walmart shoppers while promoting a “Tailgating Deserves Pepsi” campaign. The effort will also be promoted across 15 NFL team partnerships via retail, new creative and in-person experiences.

Pepsi has deepened its connection to football via retail visibility, with a 30% increase in point-of-sale presence over last year, per the brand. Pepsi has been the official soft drink of the NFL for nearly three decades. Earlier this year, the brand advertised in the Super Bowl with a 30-second national spot that featured a polar bear who is befuddled after picking Pepsi Zero Sugar over Coke Zero in a blind taste test.

PepsiCo in Q3 saw net revenue increase 5.6%, per an earnings statement. For its beverages division, the company reported improving organic volume trends, driven by strength in energy drinks, functional hydration and zero-sugar and flavored soft drinks. Still, PepsiCo is looking to trim spending as its broader North American business continues to face sales challenges amid shifting consumer habits.

This fall, KFC U.S. announced that it will replace Pepsi beverages with Coca-Cola across its restaurant system by spring 2027. The win for rival Coke comes as its Mr. Pibb beverage rises as the fastest-growing brand this year. Another rival, Keurig Dr Pepper, is planning to increase its marketing investment, potentially presenting another challenge for PepsiCo.

Correction: This piece has been updated with the proper spelling of Pepsi’s Yes Chef Tailgates program.

#7449. X adds video clipping

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The option allows users to share shorter snippets of creator content while still giving credit and allowing both posters to earn monetary rewards.

X has added another way for users to share content and ensure that original creators get credit, with the launch of its new clipping option for videos.

As shown in this example screen, now, when viewing a video on X that is 2 minutes or longer, users will be able to select “clip video” from the repost options.

With this, users can choose a specific segment of the original video to share, from 5 to 60 seconds in length (limited to 30% of the original clip). They can then re-post and add their own commentary.

The re-shared clip will include an overlay that displays the creator’s handle, while viewers of the re-shared clip will also be able to easily tap through to the full video to view the full surrounding context.

As per X: “The timestamp shows where the clip sits in the original video, such as 1:14/25:00.”

What’s more, both the creator and the sharing account will be credited with any impressions generated as a result of this process, ensuring that everyone gets an opportunity to earn from X’s Original Creator Rewards program.

This could be a valuable way to drive more video engagement and ensure that creators get more credit and exposure from re-shares of their content.

However, there are also some limitations.

At present, creators don’t have the option to turn off clipping for their videos. The only option to avoid unwanted clips is to delete the original video post, which will result in any clips generated from it also being removed from the app.

X also said that live broadcasts cannot be clipped yet.

However, the clipping tool is another means for X to build on video engagement as the platform looks to double down on what’s driving usage.

In 2023, X reported that video consumption was rapidly rising in the app, and said that it would try to capitalize on this shift with new video features.

It’s taken a couple of years, but in recent months, X has launched an updated livestream studio process, added new video overlay options and rolled out an updated video composer.

X also launched a Video Kickstart Bonus program last month, providing another means for video creators to get paid for their content.

Clipping adds yet another element, which could see more video content and related discussion flowing through X’s network.

X said that clipping is now available in both the iOS and Android versions of the app, with web access coming soon.

#7444. Meta publishes explainer on Your Algorithm controls

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The feature enables users to opt in or out of certain topics and customize their feeds based on personal preferences.

Meta has shared some new insights into how its Your Algorithm control option on Facebook works, which enables users to provide direct input into what content they want to see more or less of in the app.

The tool enables users to add or remove specific topics from an automatically generated list of interests, which Facebook's system has built based on each user's in-app actions. In addition to removing and adding topics, users can also now tell the algorithm specifically what they want to see more of, via a recently added chatbot prompt.

Conceptually, this gives users more ways to refine their Facebook experience.

On the Meta engineering blog, the company has shared notes on how the process works, and explained more about how exactly updating user algorithm preferences can impact in-app experiences.

In addition to these topic-related notes, Meta said the system also used demotion rules to enact more general parameters that don’t relate to a specific topic.

“Quality-related requests, such as reducing AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, map to dedicated demotion signals rather than topic matching,” Meta said.

These demotion rules work differently than topic ranking, with the system using these as indicators to reduce these elements.

“During ranking, the same embedding-based comparison used in the relevance check removes candidates too close to an interest in Not Interested In, and demotion rules push down near matches,” Meta said.

In other words, this feature can reduce the presence of artificial intelligence-generated content in a user’s Facebook feed, though it won’t get rid of that entirely, and ranking will still be influenced by future engagement.

When a user requests less content from a specific creator, however, “that creator’s content is filtered out directly,” Meta said.

These notes provide more insight into how Meta plans to facilitate algorithm customization and give users more control over their in-app experiences.

Meta’s hope is that through tools like this, users will feel more empowered in the app. In turn, that may quell ongoing calls for the platform to return to a reverse chronological feed and remove ranking elements entirely.

Given that algorithmic amplification has continued to drive up Facebook and Instagram usage, Meta is very keen to keep that in place.

Though the company may not have a choice. Last month, the Australian government began preliminary investigations into potential new laws that would force social media platforms to provide users with an option to switch off algorithmic recommendations and set non-algorithmic feeds as the default.

A growing body of research suggests that algorithmic amplification can have harmful impacts. If this new push in Australia goes ahead and it ends up showing that the negative impacts of algorithms are reduced, that could lead to more regions exploring similar rules.

As noted, Meta is very keen to avoid this outcome.

Last year on a Q2 earnings call with analysts, Meta CEO Mark Zukerberga said AI recommendations had led to a 5% increase in time spent on Facebook, and a 6% boost on Instagram for the quarter.

On its Q2 earnings call a year later, Zuckerberg said that global time spent on Instagram had grown in the quarter by double digits year over year, and Facebook video time spent had increased by 9% globally, "largely driven by improvements to our feed and Reels recommendations."

It makes sense, then, that Meta is keen to avoid any external push to switch off its algorithmic ranking.

As such, Meta's hoping that the introduction of this control option will ease user concerns. Combine this with the fact that, based on past history, users rarely update their settings, and the company's likely hoping that it can benefit from the perception of control afforded by the tool, while also seeing a minor impact on its business.

#7442. Synthetic audiences fall short: What marketers need to know

The AI-generated audience simulations may make it more difficult for brands to reach new audiences, writes RYA co-founder Mark Himmelsbach.

The following is a guest piece written by Mark Himmelsbach, co-founder of creative AI marketing tool RYA and advertising agency Episode Four. Opinions are the author’s own.

Artificial intelligence has proposed a novel technique for testing that’s cheaper, faster and whose proponents say is as accurate — perhaps even more so — as “real” research: synthetic audiences.

CMOs have good reasons to want this. Research is expensive, deadlines are short, marketers need to do even more with less and they increasingly need to justify their decisions using data. Synthetic audiences are simulated panels of customers, built from a set of data like customer records, interviews, demographic descriptions or combinations of those inputs.

These simulations can evaluate campaigns and explain their preferences in minutes. Marketers can then revise their work, ask again and repeat at a fraction of the cost of recruiting a human panel. But do synthetic audiences constitute high enough quality evidence?

The market seems to think so. In July, synthetic data company Simile raised $200 million at a $2 billion valuation, five months after announcing its series A. Even Adobe now lets marketers test creative, messaging and more against AI-generated customer profiles inside its Brand Intelligence product.

Now, properly identifying a target audience and codifying their preferences is hard enough. A simulation whose predictions hold up against real customer responses can help improve familiar campaigns. Indeed, for those teams who’ve successfully modeled their customers, synthetic audiences will save them considerable amounts of time and money.

There may even be additional creative possibilities on the margin — think more precise demographics, more targeted campaigns — but it basically helps you do more of the same.

A brand trying to acquire new customers, however, needs to understand people who haven’t yet made a decision to spend money with them. This is where simulations get tricky.

Synthetic audiences are being sold with that kind of solution in mind as well. Evidenza, for example, markets itself as “AI market research for impossible audiences,” as in impossible to do without AI.

But synthetic audiences still need evidence about the people they’re supposed to represent. Giving the model good evidence upon which to train is called grounding in the AI industry. For example, Bain reports that pairing simulated customers with a company’s own customer data substantially improved their overall performance.

But whose data are we talking about? What separates a useful synthetic audience from a generic simulation is data quality over time: whose experiences are represented, how recently were they observed, how relevant are they to the task at hand, and how often does new evidence get added to the training data?

A detailed snapshot of your existing customers may not actually provide much insight into potential customers who considered your brand but walked away. I’m reminded of the classic financial services industry disclosure: “past performance is not indicative of future results.”

Synthetic audiences – and synthetic data writ large – propose to use statistics and AI to create the data required to model those missed customers using external sources and observations. But again, part of the art of marketing is identifying trends and finding creative ways to stand out by doing something different that appeals to your target audience.

Whether or not AI can help humans do so is the trillion-dollar question.

Activision CMO Tyler Bahl, for example, asks what his team could do that only “Call of Duty” could do. His “stature, swagger, and scale” criteria express an ambition for the brand to delight their customers with singular, spirited ideas. A synthetic audience can help test how an idea might land, but can it decide what’s worth trying and how far to push it?

What’s more, there’s a self-reinforcing dynamic here that must be considered. Even if the data is high quality, and even if the model itself isn’t overtly biased, how might it eventually condition its users to test ideas likely to get accepted?

Constant scoring risks making a team more conservative and risk-averse rather than more creative and productive.

If campaigns need good “scores” to get approved, marketers will have every reason to learn what the panel rewards. This is commonly known as survivorship bias.

Under pressure, marketers may — consciously or not — begin incorporating those preferences before proposing something. Eventually, the process might invert: whereas the simulation was intended to improve creative decision-making, it may begin to influence creative decision-making, often regressing to the mean.

In the end, CMOs have to decide how much authority to give these tools, and leave their teams room to both use these models and pursue ideas the models wouldn’t have picked. They can thus derive considerable value from synthetic audiences while preserving the judgment and imagination that make their teams valuable. A few practical recommendations:

Cheaper, faster research should undoubtedly give creative teams more room to explore. Use simulation to test more ideas, learn from the results and improve the work. But marketing leaders must refrain from delegating too much of the process to the machines and remember to seek ways to ground their simulations in reality.

#7440. X experiments with expanded AI transparency labels

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company is testing an automated way to detect and tag posts that may have been generated using artificial intelligence.

X is developing new AI transparency labels for posts, which will not only indicate whether AI was used to generate an update, but also how it was applied in each instance.

Michael O’Herlihy, X’s head of brand safety, shared some examples of these new labels during a presentation at the Brand & AI Safety Summit in New York on Tuesday.

As shown on these example screens, posted by Adweek senior tech reporter Kendra Barnett on X, X’s new AI content labels will include more detailed information on why a post was flagged for AI content. This will better explain the rationale X’s automated enforcement system is using, while also giving creators more opportunities to refute these labels by offering them a more detailed understanding of any potential concerns.

The hope is that these expanded notes will help X refine its AI detection process by prompting more creators to provide feedback on the specifics. This information can then be used to train the system.

At the same time, the tags will add more transparency for users, who may be less likely to re-share a post that’s been flagged for AI content.

O’Herlihy added that X increased its reliance on automated tagging of AI violations because it’s much faster. The automation should also ensure that more harmful content is refuted in-stream.

It could be a good way to enhance transparency in the AI era. However, false positives could also be problematic for creators, who could get annoyed if their content is unfairly tagged.

#7437. Why Rao’s heated up brand building with a request to slow down meals

The Campbell Company sauce brand reimagines the concept of a limited-time offer by keying in on how many meals people have left with loved ones.

Rao’s Homemade today revealed a four-minute short film that reimagines the concept of a limited-time offer by reminding consumers that the most limited time is the time people spend together, per details shared with Marketing Dive. “Limited-Time Only” was directed by Aqsa Altaf and John X. Carey, the duo known as Aqsa + John X. who were behind Dove’s “Real Beauty Sketches” campaign.

“Limited-Time Only” shares the story of three individuals as they are interviewed about how often they have dinner with family. The heart-tugging video culminates with each being presented a jar of Rao’s sauce labeled with an estimate of how many meals they have left with certain family members before being surprised with a dinner with their loved ones.

The short film is part of a larger “Make Time” campaign created with Goodby Silverstein & Partners that spans premium video, social, influencer, public relations, retail media and owned channels.

In a survey of more than 1,000 individuals and in-depth interviews with 200 people, the brand and agency learned that 84% of Americans wish they shared more meals with loved ones, yet only one-third of families actually sit down together. The campaign unites those findings with product truths about the time-intensive way Rao’s sauce is made, from hand-picked tomatoes and hand-peeled onions and garlic that are simmered for hours.

“It's not just about the food; It's about the experience that creating that food enables, and it's an opportunity to really slow down and savor the food and to savor those that you're sitting around the table with, and to make meal time less of a transaction and more of an experience and an opportunity to connect with others,” said Chris Tutor, vice president of advertising and design at Rao’s parent The Campbell Company.

That experience was captured in a series of ads that feature groups of people enjoying a meal and include taglines like “the best part of the day is sharing it” and “keep long stories long.” The spots are set to live orchestral music and end with a scarpetta, the Italian tradition of using bread to mop up the last of the sauce. The creation of those spots led the team to investigate the larger narrative around meals with loved ones that informed “Limited-Time Only.”

“The long-form [video] allowed us to tell more of that story from the impetus for it to the aha moment to then the celebratory moment, and it really allowed us to blow out that visceral moment around the table into the full story,” Tutor said.

While “Limited-Time Only” does not have a traditional ad length, the creative is in line with a trend around longer-form content that marketers have adopted to tell more engaging stories to consumers. Depending on the platform, the brand will either run the long-form asset or teasers that point to the full video.

“There's been a lot of media attention around this idea, and so we’re leveraging media partners to help tell the story,” Tutor said. “Setting up the context before watching the film will also, we think, drive a lot of eyeballs to it. We're trying to do the math and science of making sure the right piece of content shows up on the right channel at the right time.”

The Campbell Company acquired Rao’s parent Sovos Brands for $2.7 billion deal in March 2024. Rao’s is a billion-dollar brand for Campbell’s and continues to grow, with consumption up 11.3% in fiscal year 2026. To fuel this growth, Rao’s increased media spending and will further increase it in fiscal 2027, executives said on a recent earnings call.

While Rao’s has grown household penetration, it still lags behind sister brand Prego. The “Make Time” campaign is key to the brand’s marketing efforts and represents both a brand building story and an awareness play.

“As people become aware of the brand or if they're already aware of the brand, what does the brand stand for beyond just that exceptional food? It's bringing this notion of slow living to every meal, reminding people that life tastes better when it's savored, and establishing what the brand means on an emotional level, versus just a rational level,” Tutor said.

#7433. Elon Musk’s Grok AI faces legal challenges over nudification

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Multiple plaintiffs allege that the chatbot is directly responsible for creating naked images based on photos taken of them as children, per Bloomberg.

Elon Musk’s xAI is facing questions regarding who is ultimately responsible for the generation of harmful content via generative artificial intelligence tools. At the heart of these issues is whether the fault lies with the person who tells the system to create this material, or the platform that facilitates this functionality.

These problems lie at the core of multiple legal cases involving xAI’s Grok chatbot, with plaintiffs in three U.S. states seeking legal recourse against xAI over the creation of CSAM material.

As reported by Bloomberg, xAI has come under investigation in three high-profile cases.

The company has denied responsibility in these cases, and said these depictions were generated by users, not by xAI itself.

Musk, xAI’s owner, has also made similar public statements.

In January, amid reports that Grok was being used to generate thousands of nudified images every day, Musk posted: “Anyone using Grok to make illegal content will suffer the same consequences as if they upload illegal content.”

However, shortly after making that announcement, and facing a potential ban of X apps from app stores, xAI changed its policies and usage restrictions on Grok to ensure that it could no longer be used to generate nudified images at scale.

The change in approach showed that xAI had the capacity to restrict this functionality whenever it wanted. However, the company instead initially refused to restrict Grok usage on free speech grounds, and settled on user autonomy as its legal defense.

Indeed, xAI has even challenged new laws designed to outlaw the generation of non-consensual naked images.

As reported by Reuters last month, xAI succeeded in blocking the implementation of Minnesota’s proposed ban on AI-generated naked images by arguing that the law was unconstitutional and infringed on free speech rights. The company was the only provider actively opposing this law.

At the same time, xAI has repeatedly touted Grok’s systematic capacity to generate what is called “spicy” content or offensive material in its “unhinged mode.” The company has also launched companion chatbots that can engage in NSFW chats.

As such, this does seem like more of a feature than a bug, yet xAI is hoping it can hang onto the fact that it’s not liable for usage that goes beyond certain stated parameters.

Establishing legal responsibility could set a new precedent in AI image generation, and it will be interesting to see whether any of these cases results in xAI being held responsible.

#7431. Priceline’s AI agent Penny lands in Snapchat ads amid holiday rush

The brand is the first in the travel category to use AI Sponsored Snaps, which allow advertisers to bring their own chatbots into Snapchat.

Priceline is trying out Snapchat’s AI Sponsored Snaps in the ramp up to a holiday season when travel is expected to be more expensive due to higher fuel costs and stubborn inflation. Average domestic round-trip airfare for Thanksgiving was up 20% year over year on Priceline as of late October, Marketing Dive’s sister publication Hotel Dive recently reported. As consumers try to stretch their dollars further, more are turning to AI tools, including personal agents, to map out their trips and find deals.

Priceline has been shoring up a brand positioning around combatting soaring travel costs. In May, it brought back its Priceline Negotiator character in ads that showed William Shatner, who played the role in memorable TV commercials from the 2000s, passing the baton to Randall Park.

The Snapchat campaign is a way for Priceline to build awareness and adoption for Penny, a conversational AI tool that the brand revamped in June. Penny at the time added capabilities from Anthropic’s Claude models as part of a transition to becoming more “fully agentic,” including the ability to handle more complex user queries and surface real-time pricing comparisons.

Snapchatters who open Priceline’s promoted Snap message and engage with Penny will be able to seek out inspiration for travel destinations, develop an itinerary and identify places to stay. Those details will be preserved for consumers who then jump to Priceline to complete their travel booking. Penny converts users at approximately twice the rate of non-Penny users on Priceline, according to the company.

Snapchat introduced AI Sponsored Snaps in April, allowing advertisers to bring their own chatbots into a high engagement chat inbox interface on the ephemeral messaging app. The format is an iteration of Sponsored Snaps, a popular ad product that drives about 22% more conversions and 20% lower cost per action compared to other inventory on the platform.

Snapchat sees a bigger opportunity in the travel category, as two-thirds of surveyed users have added a destination to their wishlist after viewing it on Snapchat. Eighty-seven percent of Snapchat users make at least one trip for leisure annually, higher than non-users of the service, per press materials.

Snapchat for the past few years has been reworking its ad suite to be more centered on performance marketing solutions that can produce business results. The app has recently seen an exodus of advertising executives while its rate of ad revenue growth has fallen short of expectations, including due to declines in upper-funnel ad products. Snapchat’s revenue derived from ads increased 4% in Q3 while total revenue was up 14% for the period.

“While advertising revenue growth remains below our ambitions, advertisers are seeing the benefits of our performance improvements,” Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said in prepared remarks ahead of the company’s Q3 earnings earlier this month. “Our focus now is to turn these improvements into broader adoption, more meaningful share of advertiser budgets and more durable growth.”

#7428. LinkedIn tests frequent viewer feature

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Premium users already see who views their profile, but a new report from Wired said the platform may also soon show how often someone stops by.

LinkedIn users may soon be able to derive more value from its “Who viewed your profile” list, with the platform working on a new feature that would not only show who visited their profile, but also how often each specific user revisited their page within a given period.

That would add more context to LinkedIn’s profile viewer data, although for most users, this is fairly useless information. However, some marketers have highlighted this as a lead-generation opportunity, providing a list of potential warm contacts, based on the fact that they’ve checked out a user’s profile.

A frequency indicator on the same display would enhance that capacity, by showing people who have returned to a user’s profile in the app again and again, which could be an indicator of even stronger interest.

So long as that interest is in a professional capacity.

A visit count for each profile listed could also show users who could be interested in them for other reasons, which could make this a somewhat unsettling display.

LinkedIn users can lock down their profile to connections only, so there would be ways to address this concern, and of course users are under no obligation to contact people who’ve visited their profile.

Wired said that LinkedIn confirmed the feature is currently in testing, but it had no further info to share at this stage.

#7426. Netflix embraces 35mm film in international campaign

“Find the Thing You Never Knew You Needed” consists of three new spots shot in different aspect ratios and a social series.

As U.S. consumers continue to cut back on subscriptions, including for streaming services, Netflix’s latest campaign emphasizes the quality of its vast content library in order to help it stand out in a crowded field. “Find the Thing You Never Knew You Needed” comes as company executives continue to put an emphasis on value and engagement following price hikes and lower projected ad revenue.

Created by Netflix’s in-house shop the Brand Creative Studio and agency Mother, the campaign features three spots shot on 35mm film using different aspect ratios. In “Axolotl,” which is shot for widescreen, an axolotl leverages its quadrupedalism to escape its tank and turn the TV back on after its owners leave in the middle of a “Bridgerton” marathon. “Dawn” follows a vampire who braves the rapidly rising sun to find a working TV in order to watch “Love Is Blind.” In “Hypersleep,” an astronaut who is the only one awake while his fellow shipmates are in cryosleep, wakes someone up in order to show them the “Soda Pop” scene from “KPop Demon Hunters.”

The spots were directed by Vania Heymann and Gal Muggia of the production company Iconoclast. The nature of the ads allows for the featured program to be swapped out depending on the market. In Brazil, the show featured in “Dawn” is crime drama “Os Donos Do Jogo,” or “Rulers of Fortune” in English.

Over the course of four episodes, the social series “Typecast” will feature four creatives and showcase their somewhat unexpected Netflix fixations. The series kicks off with fashion designer Willy Chavarria and his show of choice “Love on the Spectrum.” Other guests include musician Teezo Touchdown, makeup artist Isamaya Ffrench and Randy Savvy of The Compton Cowboys. The videos were filmed in 16mm to fit the feel of the overall campaign.

The campaign’s use of analog film is part of a recent trend that has seen advertisers looking to run counter to the rise of artificial intelligence. Stop-motion animation has been of particular interest, with brands such as Levi’s and Prada embracing the artform. Netflix’s spots, which feature custom-built sets, follow a similar vein of appealing to the desire for human-made advertising.

Netflix grew revenue 12% year over year to $12.9 billion in Q3, per an earnings release. The company lowered its expected ad revenue for the year from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, a drop it attributed to a slower-than-expected rollout of some advertising capabilities.

#7423. Thought leadership remains highly valuable for B2B buyers

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A new report from Edelman examined content on LinkedIn and found that brands value professional insight and experience from other professionals.

Edelman has published a new report which examines the impact of thought leadership content on LinkedIn, and how professionals are utilizing thought leader content within their decision-making process.

Based on insights from “more than 1,100 management-level professionals,” Edelman’s 2026 B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report provides notes on the shifting B2B landscape. In particular, it looks at the role professional expertise plays in the artificial intelligence era.

According to the report, that role is still significant.

Edelman’s data showed that 82% of buyers believe that thought leadership is becoming more valuable, with original research, insight and experience now being more of a differentiator.

The data also showed that 89% of buyers view high-quality thought leadership content “makes a company feel like a long-term partner worth choosing.”

What’s more, a brand that doesn’t share thought leadership content can risk being eliminated from consideration for some potential partners.

And while AI tools are now playing a bigger role in the discovery process, the data also showed that most buyers still validate AI recommendations by referring to a brand’s content.

Also worth noting: Buyers are more likely to share thought leadership content in private channels.

There are also some interesting notes on the value of external influencers when it comes to endorsing a business, and the importance of brands continuing to produce thought leadership content to reinforce existing partnerships.

In summary, while product research is changing, and more business buyers are using AI tools to find relevant products, original brand content still plays a key role in winning deals and assuring buyers that they’re making the right decision.

The key differentiation, then, is expertise and unique insight that nobody else can provide. Even in the age of AI, where digital systems can summarize information,  AI can’t provide real, hands-on experience and insights. It also can’t summarize information that doesn’t already exist.

Hence the need for more thought leadership-type content, and for brands to differentiate themselves through expanded sharing of their professional expertise.

#7421. Carnival gamifies cruise experience via interactive Twitch livestream

Streamer iJustine will take on a series of challenges voted on by viewers as she explores a digital Carnival Celebration ship.

Carnival is turning to Twitch to give consumers a unique look at what a trip aboard one of its vessels would entail at a time when the demographics of the average cruise passenger are in flux. The activation comes as the company reported record-high bookings for 2027 and a net income of $1.9 billion in the third quarter, an all-time high for the company. However, gross margin yields fell 1.3%  due to high fueling costs, per an earnings release.

Cruising has become more popular than ever, with a record 22.4 million Americans expected to take a cruise in 2027, up 3.6% year over year, per AAA research. The pre-pandemic total for American cruise travelers was 14.2 million. While the vacation choice is stereotypically associated with older demographics, the average age of an American cruiser is 45.8, and millennials and Gen Z travelers are increasingly drawn to the travel method due to lower costs and value-oriented packages, according to AAA research.

The livestream will feature a custom-built game in which iJustine, who has nearly 55,000 followers on Twitch at press time, will tackle challenges on the simulated Carnival Celebration. The ship’s spaces and activities, as well as destinations from the brand’s Paradise Destinations collection, will be part of the gameplay. Along with input from the audience, Weigand will help keep energy high by introducing challenges, passing on requests from viewers and offering community instructions. iJustine, who will be playing live onboard, will work to earn her cruise director badge and a Fun Meter will track energy levels.The game is over once the meter hits zero.

To encourage participation, audience members will have the chance to win a cruise vacation. The full livestream will be posted to Instagram and TikTok the day after the event so fans can catch up on what they missed. The game will not be made available to the public after the stream.

“We’re constantly looking for new ways to push the boundaries on how we connect with consumers, and Play Carnival takes that thinking to a whole new level,” said Michael Sotelo, vice president of brand, product and social media at Carnival Cruise Line, in press materials.

The effort falls under the “Find Your Fun Again” campaign, which encourages consumers to ditch the stress and monotony of everyday life and find joy aboard a Carnival ship. Actor Nick Offerman took center stage in a spot in which he goes on vacation after smashing his phone due to receiving an overload of notifications.

Amazon-owned platform Twitch has become a go-to for brands looking to experiment with connecting with young consumers. Last year, E.l.f. Cosmetics became the first brand to test Twitch’s livestream shopping ads.

#7416. Maybelline updates ‘Maybe’ tagline as beauty perceptions evolve

Miley Cyrus is leading a new global brand platform promoting changes meant to be more inclusive and empowering for women.

Maybelline is reworking one of its signature brand assets as it tries to adapt to an evolving landscape for beauty and cosmetics. The L'Oréal-owned marketer’s “Maybe she’s born with it” tagline became a fixture of its advertising beginning in 1991, but consumers in 2026 are applying makeup for different reasons.

The company has attempted to modernize “Maybe” in the past. It was at one point dropped for the largely forgotten “Make It Happen” but eventually brought back. Maybelline revamped the “Maybe” tagline for the TikTok era two years ago. The latest overhaul appears more substantial, changing the underlying meaning of the copy, and is described in the release as permanent.

Over half of surveyed global respondents today see beauty as a way to build confidence compared to 26% who see it as a means of looking more attractive to other people or appearing younger for longer, per McKinsey findings cited by Maybelline. The suggestion is that makeup can be something less superficial and more empowering and inclusive.

Tweaks to the marketer’s tagline try to recognize these trends by adjusting the phrasing to sound less like a question being asked about a single woman’s look. Instead, the new “Maybe” is positioned as a declaration of the possibilities all women can achieve by leveraging makeup as a form of self-expression.

“With 'Maybe.', we're building on our legacy and inviting women everywhere, at every stage of life, to explore the possibilities within them,” said Maybelline Global Brand President Sandrine Jolly in a statement.

Maybelline enlisted Cyrus, an ambassador who’s previously voiced the “Maybe” tagline, to lead its new “The Beauty of Infinite Possibility” platform. Cyrus was selected for the effort because her own career has entailed a constantly shifting identity, moving from child star to hard-partying club song purveyor and then back to her country roots.

Cyrus released her latest album, “Bass Persuades,” in September, which could draw additional interest to the Maybelline partnership. “Bass Persuades” sees Cyrus again dabbling in the dance pop and electronic music genres.

Products featured in the campaign include Maybelline’s Serum Lipstick, Lash Sensational Sky High Mascara and Instant Eraser Concealer. Maybelline will partner with additional women in the worlds of music and elsewhere to share their stories of using makeup as a form of expression and reinvention.

Consumer products, the division of L'Oréal that Maybelline sits under, grew 4.3% on a like-for-like basis in Q3, lagging other segments like dermatological beauty and professional products.

#7414. Amid a difficult transitional year, The Trade Desk posts a rare quarterly revenue decline

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

The latest batch of ad tech earnings disclosures was made public after the bell yesterday, with The Trade Desk posting a rare annual revenue decrease, only the second in its decade as a publicly listed company, and a sign of the scale of its turnaround challenges.

The industry’s largest independent demand-side platform, whose immediate rivals are Amazon and Google, recently trumpeted the return of The Trade Desk cofounder and CTO Dave Pickles to help mount its comeback after a challenging 18-to-24 months.

The DSP posted Q3 revenue of $736 million, representing a 0.5% annual dip – the last such dip occurred at the depths of business uncertainty during the Covid-19 pandemic – a sign of the scale of the turnaround challenge it faces.

Meanwhile, its ad tech cohorts posted revenue increases during the reporting period on the same day (see chart below), another sign of the sector’s mixed fortunes.

Jeff Green, cofounder and CEO, The Trade Desk, noted the company’s reorganization efforts of the last year, which included a 15% headcount cut during Q3, plus its third-party audience and agentic offerings, plus its plans for more transparent measurement for advertisers. “I’m extremely excited to have him [Pickles] more deeply engaged with the team as we move into this next chapter,” Green told analysts, “we spent the last year changing our company because the industry has changed and is continuing to change.”

Execs there pointed out that revenue performance during the period was “meaningfully ahead of the outlook we provided,” noting how video, including CTV, now accounts for more than half of its revenue mix, with the DSP also forecasting that its Q4 revenue would be “at least $755 million.”

In a prepared statement, Jeff Green said, “We are moving with greater urgency across the company,” but acknowledged, “we are still operating below the level of growth we expect from ourselves.”

Facing questions from analysts, Green later outlined the company’s planned tactical changes, as well as when it expects to return to more sustainable growth, noting how the company needs to “make the power of The Trade Desk easier to use, easier to adopt and easier to prove incremental outcomes.”

He added, “Open measurement is expected to better prove incremental outcomes… while open measurement will be implemented this quarter, we expect the product to improve our growth next year and provide a tailwind for years to come.”

Under further questioning from analysts, Green noted how The Trade Desk – a company that has been notably reticent over mergers and acquisitions – was more open than ever to M&A given the current technological landscape.

However, that shouldn’t be mistaken for a change in the company’s attitude to writing checks for more ad tech, even if it does lead to more lines of business. “Our philosophy on M&A has not fundamentally changed,” he told analysts.

“We’re looking [at M&A prospects] more now than we historically have, but that said, it’s also critical to take away that our standards are also higher than ever,” Green said, adding that his leadership would never want to “derail” its current trajectory “simply because we bought a company.”

Green’s comments came the same afternoon as Zeta Global posted revenue of $493 million, up 46% year on year, making it one of the fastest-growing companies in terms of revenue throughout the period, with the company further raising its Q4 revenue guidance to the range of $521 million to $525 million, a figure that would represent up to 33% annual growth.

Meanwhile, rival DSP Viant posted $110.4 million in Q3 revenue, a 29% annual increase, as well as the purchase of generative AI company Waymark, with management noting they expected Q4 revenue in the region of $130.5 million to $133.5 million.

Elsewhere, supply-side platform PubMatic posted revenue of $79.6 million, up 17% year on year, with company leadership keen to underline an ongoing industry trend that many feel is helping to bring more equity to the historic power imbalance between the buy- and sell-side of the industry.

“AI is accelerating the shift from sell-side targeting to sell-side decisioning, enabling buyers to act on richer intelligence closer to the inventory and first party [sic] insights,” noted Rajeev Goel, PubMatic CEO, in a prepared statement, which also forecast Q4 revenue in the range of $91 to $93 million, a prospective increase of 15%.

#7412. Fetch trades views for rewards with brand-backed holiday microseries

“The Receipt” features brands like Dove, Breyer’s and Olipop across six episodes and offers consumers points for viewing that can be redeemed for gift cards.

Fetch is angling to become a more integral part of the holiday shopping experience with what it bills as the industry’s first rewarded romantic comedy. The effort leverages an in-app rewarded video format launched by Fetch in August alongside WPP Media, which helped bring the tool to market, and Unilever, which served as a launch partner. In early tests of the format, Fetch observed a 96% video completion rate, per details shared in the launch announcement.

Privately-owned Fetch operates by allowing consumers to upload receipts from everyday purchases to earn points that can be exchanged for gift cards. The company sees over 13 million receipts submitted each day and has awarded over $1 billion in points to date, per release details. Over the holidays, Fetch expects consumers to redeem over $100 million in rewards, said founder and CEO Wes Schroll in a press statement.

“The Receipt” follows the story of Chloe, played by Condor, after a meet-cute with Max, played by De La Torre — Condor’s real-life husband — results in a tote bag swap. To reconnect with Max, Chloe relies on shopping receipts found in his bag and the help of best friend Liam, played by Sedeño, a creator with nearly 1.5 million followers on TikTok. The series, created with director Michael Hoy, also features creators from Fetch’s Creator Club ambassador program.

New episodes of the series will launch every three days until Dec. 18 on Fetch’s Instagram, YouTube and TikTok channels. Each episode will feature a single brand partner, with participants including Olipop, Breyers, Dove, health food brand Kize and CPG manufacturing company Nehemiah, a close partner of Procter & Gamble. General Mills brands Betty Crocker and Blue Buffalo will be featured together in one episode. The featured brands will each be tied into a storyline in the series, pushing past traditional product placement in a move that could drive stronger brand recall among viewers.

Within the Fetch app, consumers can watch the series trailer, which launches Nov. 20, and episodes to earn points that can be redeemed for gift cards. Users can also earn points by shopping the episodes within the in-app Fetch Shop, or complete Fetch Play gaming challenges to unlock bonus content.

The global cashback apps market was valued at $6.12 billion last year and is expected to grow to nearly $12 billion by 2034 as consumers attempt to make their dollars stretch further. Average household spending over the 2026 holiday season is expected to reach $1,654, a 4% increase over the year-ago period, according to Deloitte.

The latest effort from Fetch taps into the growing trend around branded microdramas and episodic content. Others that have leveraged a similar strategy recently include L’Oréal’s Urban Decay, Marc Jacobs and JCPenney.

#7411. Ad Tech Briefing: Amazon’s auction trial puts agentic advertising’s trust problem in focus

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →

Amazon, along with its Big Tech cohorts, wants advertisers to trust its AI more, but fresh allegations from federal regulators underline concerns over such platforms.

Last week, the Federal Trade Commission published newly unredacted details from its lawsuit accusing Amazon of secretly inflating advertising prices, with similar charges against Google still fresh in the public mindset.

According to the FTC, Amazon imposed surcharges of up to 50% on ordinary shopping days and 250% during major retail events, generating an additional $87 million during the 2022 holiday season. Amazon disputes the allegations, and the legal proceedings are ongoing.

Amazon recently reported quarterly advertising revenue approaching $20 billion, with  Amazon Ads Agent – an AI-powered platform that’s likely to attract accusations of “black box” from detractors – a key part of its push to automate campaign planning, buying and optimization.

And with Amazon, the third pillar of adland’s triopoly, the key question for advertisers is whether they should hand over more control to a platform when they cannot independently verify how its existing auctions determine prices.

The FTC and 22 state attorneys general accuse Amazon of misleading advertisers about its Sponsored Products auctions.

Amazon presented these as generalized second-price auctions, where advertisers generally pay prices determined by competing bids rather than their maximum bid.

However, regulators allege Amazon introduced undisclosed reserve-price mechanisms that increased charges without corresponding competition, effectively pushing prices closer to first-price auctions.

According to the government body’s allegations, during the 2021 holiday season, Amazon increased average cost per click by 20%, with some advertisers seeing increases exceeding 200%. The complaint also alleges executives considered using reserve prices to address a $40 million revenue shortfall.

The allegations extend to how Amazon explained rising prices, i.e., whether Amazon misrepresented how its auctions worked and what advertisers were charged.

However, Amazon maintains that reserve prices reflect the value of its advertising placements, disputes the FTC’s interpretation, and argues that reserve pricing is not inherently unlawful.

For advertisers, the concern is straightforward: they can see what they paid, but cannot necessarily establish how that price was calculated.

The allegations come shortly after Amazon introduced new products designed to automate more advertising decisions.

At October’s unBoxed conference, Amazon unveiled Ads Agent and Full-Funnel Campaigns, allowing advertisers to set objectives, products, creative and budgets while its technology handles targeting, allocation and optimization.

Amazon says beta testing delivered up to 67% higher return on long-term ad spend and 29% lower costs per new-to-brand customer compared with manually configured campaigns. Those figures are company-reported.

The proposition is that advertisers can reduce manual campaign management and improve performance. However, greater automation also means relying more heavily on Amazon to explain how budgets are spent and why its systems make particular decisions.

While the FTC’s allegations concern Sponsored Products auctions, not Amazon’s new AI products, they still add weight to concerns raised about advertisers’ ability to inspect automated decisions, verify results, and understand fees.

Google’s ad tech antitrust case provides a precedent, although the conduct and markets differ.

A federal court found Google illegally monopolized publisher ad-serving and ad exchange markets – in a separate case, its search practices were also found to be monopolistic. The subsequent remedies stopped short of divestiture but imposed measures intended to improve competition and interoperability.

Both cases concern platforms whose control over advertising infrastructure limits customers’ ability to scrutinize how transactions work.

The difference is that Amazon is now asking advertisers to give its technology greater control over buying decisions, even as regulators challenge the transparency of its existing auction practices. These developments involve different businesses and issues, but they point to a broader accountability problem in digital advertising.

“We’re having to look much more closely at what happens after the click and whether those clicks are actually producing qualified leads and revenue.”

— Lindsay Marty, founder of Above the Bar Marketing, speaking to Digiday about advertisers reassessing their Google Search budgets.

ChatGPT’s ad offering may be on the rise, but the nature of its value is still hard to determine, according to numbers analyzed in recent studies.

#7407. Can web users trust ad tech’s server-side shift?

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

“Trust” is one of those words that gets thrown around a lot in ad tech circles. But it’s going to become even more important if ad tech completes its server-side shift.

In response to Apple’s identity resolution crackdown, the online ad industry has rallied around server-side ways to sidestep browser-based controls. IAB Tech Lab’s Trusted Server is the biggest example of this. Not only does the open-source software promise publishers faster page-load speeds, it enables publishers to better control their ad tech stacks and minimize their exposure to browser-based blockades.

Taking ad calls out of the browser, however, has the effect of taking them out of users’ sights. A browser can see – and block – the calls a web page asks it to make. Once the calls run on a publisher’s server, though, users have to trust the publisher to a greater degree.

And this is where the trust in Trusted Server really matters.

Lam also noted that Trusted Server was designed from the start to support integration with consent management platforms. That would give websites a way to share a user’s consent status across the programmatic supply chain. But of course, that requires the user blindly trusting the site to do so.

Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

“There is a fear of just broadly server-side because it’s not automatically observable to the consumer’s browser and you can’t automatically inspect it from that point. But what we’ve done for Trusted Server in particular is we’ve made sure all of this is considered. What’s included in Trusted Server is pretty robust logging and auditing. Anyone who is looking to deploy Trusted Server gets that out of the box.”

#7405. How Unilever’s social-first marketing is evolving amid reorganization

Leandro Barreto will be promoted to chief growth and marketing officer on Jan. 1, a move that’s in line with how other marketing leaders are adding responsibility for the P&L.

After seeing strong sales and volume growth last quarter, Unilever upgraded its outlook for the rest of 2026 and now expects at least 3% underlying volume growth for the full year. But the CPG giant is not standing still as it looks to build on that growth: At an investor event last week, the company announced plans to roll out a reorganized operating model in 2027 that will be centered around a “global strategy, local execution” principle.

Unilever’s operations will be split into six global units, with leadership responsible for, among other things, managing the growing convergence of content, media and commerce. In addition, Leandro Barreto, currently chief marketing officer of Unilever and its beauty and wellbeing business, will be appointed chief growth and marketing officer on Jan. 1, a move that’s in line with how other marketing leaders are adding responsibility for the P&L.

The reorganization arrives as Unilever continues to evolve into a pure-play home and personal care company following the separation of its ice cream business last year and the planned spinoff of its food business as part of a $44.8 billion deal with McCormick. The latter hit an antitrust snag in the U.K. this week that Unilever described as an “expected step” in the process.

Moving forward, Unilever plans to focus on four pillars when operating its brands: increasing the role of wellness, developing authority systems, executing flawlessly and remaining committed to a marketing philosophy it implemented last year called SASSY, which is an acronym for superior science, aesthetics, sensorials, shared by others and young spirited principles.

The “shared by others” part of SASSY includes the company’s work to shift half of digital ad spend to social-first and creator-driven marketing. Unilever reported that it now relies on 500,000 content creators, up from the previously reported 300,000 and significantly more than the 20,000 utilized before CEO Fernando Fernandez joined the company.

“We have embraced social-first marketing at a very significant speed, and this is showing in the way we are growing our key brands,” Fernandez said at Unilever’s investor event on Nov. 4. “Some of our brands have been really rejuvenated… Have we done it in all our portfolio? No. We have great examples, and we have brands in which we are starting to replicate this model.”

Currently, authority systems in a content-overloaded, artificial intelligence-powered world mediated by agentic shopping and LLMs represent a gap in Unilever’s strategy and an area where some competitors have outperformed the company.

“The algorithms have to follow a logic, and the logic they follow is geographical proximity, independent recommendation, clinical proof, patents published, ratings and review. This plays in favour of great brands with great science, with great budgets,” Fernandez explained.

AI is affecting Unilever’s business in a variety of ways, including shifting the innovation process from primarily being a physical discipline to a digital one. The company can now develop consumer signals into validated concepts in hours instead of months.

“We now can see very clearly how the signals are operating, and we can, with synthetic audiences, not only spot more than 60,000 consumer signals in a continuous way, but we also can sharpen those ideas before even real consumers see them,” Barreto said during the investor event. “The innovation also is leveraging way more data points, more than 25 million of them. That's why we can match the formulation with the concept, and we can have predictions on performance and consumer appeal.”

Unilever’s social-first marketing model involves four areas at scale: recommendation, content, influence and media. To solve for recommendation that is mediated by LLMs, Unilever said it is structuring its data to be machine-readable, working with partners like Google and optimizing by tracking more than one million prompts across more than 30 markets. In the last six months, Unilever has improved in more than 90% of the brand market sales positions that it tracks.

The company is using an AI-powered engine to meet the scale and speed of its content needs, and reports that it is producing twelve times more content than in 2024 at a 90% lower cost. In some cases, purchase intent and brand recall have increased, due in part to training AI on each brand’s DNA and core proposition. AI is also helping Unilever find, brief, vet and measure creators whose content yields ROI that is 1.5-times higher than brand-led content.

The proliferation of AI is also one of the factors reducing the lifespan of video content to four days. After that time, content on platforms like Meta, Google, TikTok, Amazon and Walmart has negative — not simply diminishing — levels of return, making marketers like Unilever rethink how it approaches content.

“The level of engagement that you provide to the platform fundamentally changes the price you pay. This is a fundamental change and makes development of content such an important capability in a company these days,” Fernandez said.

Unilever said it has dramatically reduced the cost per unit of content and improved its return on investment between 10% and 15% per year. However, that ROI is not expected to return to the company’s P&L or bottom line, but serve as a cost of doing business in a digital media environment.

“In the past, a company like Unilever could gain a significant competitive advantage by purchasing large amounts of media from TV Globo in Brazil. Today, however, media is being purchased through Meta, Google, Amazon, Walmart and TikTok, and that model no longer favors scale of purchase. Instead, it favors the quality of engagement you generate on the platform,” Fernandez said. “I believe improving our return on investment is fundamental to keeping our business model working, continuing to drive top-line growth and delivering modest margin expansion every year.”

#7404. Reddit dangles seasonal ad credits but advertisers still want better proof it works all year round

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Reddit is offering advertisers extra incentives to spend in Q4 — the stretch of the year when budgets are biggest and competition for them is fiercest.

The social news website is offering new advertisers credits on new campaigns that go live before November 20: in the U.K., they get £500 for spending £1,000, or £2,000 for spending £2,000, according to an ad exec who recently spoke with their Reddit rep and shared an email confirming the incentives and deadline. In the U.S., the platform is also offering new advertisers $1,500 in ad credits when they spend $1,500 on the platform, per ads seen by Digiday.

After reviewing the incentives that Digiday had seen, Accuracast’s group CEO Farhad Divecha said that incentives like this “do work to reignite dormant clients’ interest to retry the platform.” However, following the decline in Google Search referrals, the general sentiment among his team’s clients is that Reddit isn’t as attractive without ChatGPT and Google sending it all that traffic.

The dip Divecha is referring to is the one Reddit disclosed on its earnings call last month when CEO Steve Huffman said October search referrals were down by more than one million a week on average, in part because of Google’s AI search features. To be clear, the credits aren’t tied to the slump. Q4 incentives are a fixture of the platform ad calendar and Reddit’s deadline for them is timed to get new campaigns running before Black Friday. That said, the extra spend could still help offset some of the hit from search, at least for a quarter.

Because incentives only go so far. Keeping advertisers around once the credits run out takes an ads platform that does what marketers need it to do, from measurement to targeting to self-serve tools. Reddit is still building toward all of that.

“Reddit is making big strides to compete with their competitor set within social with new capabilities, features across targeting, bidding and measurement but ultimately still comes in last place,” said independent ad tech consultant Jonathan D’Souza Rauto. “Advertisers do like to test the waters with it but it doesn’t necessarily translate in always-on budgets.”

The incentives come at the end of a year in which the rate of Reddit’s ad revenue growth has slowed down over three consecutive quarters. In Q1 2026, Reddit recorded $625 million in ad revenue, up 74% year over year, per the company’s earnings reports. By Q2, ad revenue had increased to $762 million, the rate of growth had slipped to 64% on the same period a year ago. By Q3 2026, the platform announced $847 million in ad revenue, with growth falling again to 54% versus the same period a year ago, per its latest earnings.

“The slowdown in ad revenue growth and referral traffic may be occurring at the same time, but that doesn’t necessarily mean one is driving the other,” said Jessica Dervyn, senior principal analyst in Gartner’s Marketing Practice.

Reddit, however, points to its continued revenue growth and advertiser demand as evidence that the platform remains an attractive proposition for marketers.

“The numbers speak for themselves: we’ve grown ad revenue by more than 50% year over year for nine straight quarters, well ahead of most peers over the same timeframe,” said Natalie Maguire, director of global B2B communications at Reddit in an emailed statement to Digiday. “We continue to see strong demand from advertisers as they increasingly turn to Reddit to drive results across the funnel. Our ad incentive program has stayed consistent over the last year and we have not increased our incentives amount. It’s an ongoing part of our business and a standard practice across the industry.”

It’s a thought not lost on some advertisers.

Take James Mortimer at Roast, for example. He said that his team finds the platform “really valuable” for advertisers because the users are so engaged.

“There’s quite a lot of people on there [Reddit] you can’t reach on Meta,” he said. Mortimer acknowledged that Reddit isn’t for every advertiser, but said it was “definitely valuable for the right advertisers that can work on there.”

However, audience engagement alone isn’t necessarily enough to convince advertisers to shift more of their budgets to Reddit. Measurement remains an important part of the equation.

“That’s something where Meta is really good now, so it’s harder to make the case for a client who is spending on Meta already to then take budget and put it into another channel [like Reddit], which might not be as effective,” said Mortimer.

New Gen’s strategy director Mark Bellamy had a similar take, saying that search referrals are part of the story but not the main thing holding back ad spend on Reddit. The bigger picture, he said, is the ad product.

“Reddit is still a test-and-learn platform for us, not somewhere we’d confidently put full-funnel budget,” he said. “You can get good CPMs and decent awareness. What we haven’t seen enough of is proof that you can build an ecosystem there that drives quality traffic and nurtures it. Until we do, we’ll be cautious about recommending significant media spend.”

That puts the onus on Reddit to demonstrate that advertisers can get meaningful returns from the platform beyond the initial incentive. While promotional offers can bring new advertisers through the door, converting those trials into long-term investment is a different challenge entirely.

#7401. The case for and against AI token capping

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

When one of the world’s most valuable companies starts to get serious about AI waste, it’s time to pay attention. Apple is placing a hard cap of $200 on its engineers’ daily AI token use, and may reduce non-engineers’ token allowance to $25, Bloomberg reported last week (Nov. 4).

A handful of ad agencies have already embraced token capping this year — using AI software, or a bespoke tool, to prevent users from consuming more than a set amount of AI compute as the costs of AI transformation become clearer. Apple’s policy change indicates that more companies could follow that path, but there are tradeoffs involved in this strict approach to costs.

Agencies considering capping token usage must weigh up the risk they could douse their employees’ creativity by limiting their access to the tech.

AI costs — from tokens to licensing and subscriptions — are likely as cheap as they’ll ever be. While manageable today, they’re kept low because of the enormous capital expenditures of companies like Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. Eventually, those firms will want a return on those investments, meaning today’s prices might not be stable for long.

With that in mind, marketing agencies are building the infrastructure of AI accountability today, rather than wait for a crisis. Performance agency Roast, for example, has capped the amount of AI tokens its staffers can use since March.

“It’s up to the individual to use those tokens responsibly, and I think the benefit of that is then it’s making people think about what use cases they use tokens for,” John Campbell, head of innovation and AI at Roast, told Digiday.

The company allots a set amount of tokens to each employee within its Claude subscription, Campbell said. Higher individual caps can be provided at particularly busy times. He noted that the limit had stopped some users from relying on the tech for repetitive tasks that might be better delegated to non-AI software tools.

Video and image production generally represents the most token-intensive activity for creative agencies; media agencies experimenting with agentic tools for planning and buying must also grapple with runaway operating costs.

U.S. media agency PMG places a $50 daily limit on staff AI usage through its Alli4U portal. Staff that hit the cap more than once can be assigned a larger token budget, or receive advice on using different AI models, Dillon Larberg, consulting and strategy director, told Digiday in September. “That provides us a human in the loop moment to meet with teams or meet with individuals,” he said.

While agencies might still want to allow staff the flexibility to experiment and play with AI tools they can use tiered capping systems to provide teams with enough leeway to pilot something new, without burning up the budget.

“If you say you have a limit of $30, $25, $10 a day, you’ll find people become very creative in how they get this stuff done based on that constraint,” said Jonathan Whiteside, global executive vp at Dept, which caps team AI usage rather than individual costs.

“Constraints are sometimes useful for us to find new ways of working,” Whiteside added. “People start to think much more carefully about, ‘Well, do I actually need to use AI to do this?’”

AI costs, including the price of tokens, won’t stay low forever, so agencies should make hay while the sun’s shining. Intentionally cutting back before compute costs rise would be like abstaining from MoviePass or WeWork in the glorious days of zero interest rates. Agencies can chew through tokens while they develop the best uses for AI tech now, while it’s cheap to do so.

Some agencies use soft AI caps, rather than a hard limit. “When someone maxes out their spend for that tier, they show their work and their output to their department head,” explained Daniel Gilbert, CEO of Brainlabs, in September. He described the company’s approach as one that embraced “checkpoints” rather than caps. “The department head goes through the work with them, and if it’s good work, then they push them into the next tier.”

Such an approach preserves staff autonomy while keeping a lid on AI spending for agencies that want to to let a hundred flowers, or AI agents, bloom.

There are also means of nudging staff into cost-conscious AI decisions, without placing concrete limits on their usage. Gateway systems, or “gating,” refers to a tool which reroutes a user from a token-intensive AI model to a less powerful (and cheaper) model, if it’s better suited to a user’s project. If they’re using ChatGPT to draft their LinkedIn posts, they probably don’t need Astra, its latest and most powerful model.

Whiteside said that model selection is “a big factor” in keeping costs down, but that gating systems or staff training can provide a more appropriate guardrail than an individual token allowance.

As the real costs of AI-enabled marketing no services become clearer, expect more agencies and brands to consider whether hard caps or flexibility are most important.
